It’s 3:17 AM, and the room is quiet except for the hum of the fan and the occasional flicker of the window air conditioner that sounds like an old lawnmower trying to start. I’ve been staring at the same sentence for fifteen minutes—something about the way the light hits the walls in certain apartments during winter afternoons, when the sun is too low and everything glows like amber glass. But I can’t quite get it right. Words feel slippery tonight, like trying to grip water in a glove. So instead, I’ll let them spill without structure.

This is the kind of moment where everything feels provisional.

You ever notice how the past is just a ghost made of stories we keep telling ourselves? Like the time I convinced myself that a stray cat following me home from the grocery store was a sign. It turned out to be the chattiest, most entitled cat I’ve ever met, yowling at my window at dawn until I surrendered scraps of chicken. I named him Stanley, which might’ve been projecting—who names their cat Stanley? But he answered to it, and for three years, he thought he was the CEO of our tiny Brooklyn apartment. He’d sit on the toilet lid while I showered, judging me, tails flicking like a metronome counting my failures. When he died—poisoned by something he shouldn’t have eaten, probably a neighbor’s dumbass decision to leave rat poison in its ceramic bowl disguised as fettuccine—I framed his collar, the one with the little bell that sounded like a wind chime during midday naps. I still have it in my desk drawer. His ashes are buried in a shoebox behind the Korean deli. Every time I walk past it, I wonder if Stanley’s spirit is running the deli now, swatting at customers with the same disdain he had for me.

Grief is just memory with a neon vest on.

I think about how people tend to romanticize certain versions of themselves. Like, I like to tell people I was a “struggling artist” in my early twenties, but the truth is, I was a 24-year-old with $12,000 in student debt, a roommate who microwaved fish in our shared kitchen until the smell permeated every fabric surface, and a part-time job at a bookstore where I spent most of my shifts alphabetizing tarot decks and pretending not to notice when Karen from accounting walked out with *The Secret* under her arm. None of that sounds like a poverty-stricken revolutionary writer cultivating their soul. It sounds like a person who sneezed too much at work and cried in the stockroom because no one showed up to their poetry reading—except for Dave, who only came because he thought it was a joke and then asked why the poems were so short.

The art world is full of people who either believe their shit doesn’t stink or are so ashamed of their shit that they cover it in gold leaf and call it conceptual.

But here’s the thing: sometimes art *is* gold leaf on shit, and sometimes it’s just… shit. Distilled essence. A reflection. A way to stop the screaming in your head for five minutes. The critic who called me derivative in an anonymous blog post—the same guy who once reviewed a multi-media exhibit about urban decay by saying “the artist captures the melancholy of the concrete jungle in a way that resonates” probably has no idea that six months later I received a residency offer in Lisbon because someone on the panel had been too high on airport wine to Google me. So much of artistic reputation isn’t built on merit. It’s built on who you know, how well you can storytell your own narrative, and whether you have the audacity to charge $200 for an unprimed canvas splattered with wine and tears.

I once met a painter who only worked in the color pink. Not rose gold, not blush, but the exact shade of Pepto-Bismol. She had a gallery show where she painted the entire space that color, including the ceiling, and then sat in the middle dressed in matching pink sweatpants holding a giant paddle made of foam. She called it *Self-Conscious* and sold the paddle for $12,000. I asked her why she committed to such a specific aesthetic, and she said, “Because pink is the color of the void between ambition and reality, and I wanted to embody it.” I said, “That’s profound and also kind of stupid,” and she laughed so hard she nearly cried. We became friends. She later dated a guy who only wore beige and believed in “vibrational energy healing,” so obviously my standards were pretty low by that point.

Art thrives in contradiction.

There’s a bench by the Hudson River where I go when I need to remember that the sky used to be bigger before the city got its claws in it. Early summer evenings, the ferries leaving their docks leave long trails of orange lichen on the water, like God's wet finger painting. I sit there sometimes with strangers who aren’t strangers—same moon-faced woman who knits scarves for stray cats, and a retired dockworker who carries a thermos of black coffee that smells like motor oil and regret. We don’t talk, or if we do, it’s about the weather or how the price of cigarettes went up again. But we share space in a way that feels like community, even if it’s temporary. I like temporary communities. They don’t ask for commitment. They don’t require you to be someone you’re not.

I think a lot about impermanence these days.

My phone buzzed an hour ago with a notification: “Your mom tried to FaceTime.” I didn’t answer. There are conversations we keep rescheduling in our lives. Some are honest—death, loss, regret. Others are just bad timing. “We should catch up” messages from old friends who haven’t answered a text in three years. The DMs from people who say “You’re really insightful,” but only when they’re drunk. The emails from charities asking for donations after you Googled “existential dread” at 2 AM. These are all failed connections, like Wi-Fi signals disappearing as you walk into the bathroom.

But then there are the people who show up consistently, not despite your flaws, but because of them. My best friend Lily, who lives three hours away but still calls me every Sunday at exactly 3:15 PM because she respects my chaotic schedule like I respect her ability to eat an entire pizza in one sitting without shame. Or my therapist, Dr. Chen, who once looked me dead in the eye and said, “You’re not depressed. You’re just bored with your own life narrative.” She wasn’t wrong. I resent that she wasn’t wrong. But I keep going back because sometimes the mirror needs to be held up by someone who won’t let you look away.

I think the thing I’ve learned about writing—real writing, the kind that isn’t just journaling or therapy or performance—is that it’s not about having something to say. It’s about having the courage to say it badly. The poet Ocean Vuong once said (or I’m paraphrasing, because who remembers exact quotes) that the worst thing you can do as a writer is to try to sound intelligent. Be honest instead. Apologize later.

That’s why I’m writing this badly now.

I remember the first time I read my own words aloud in a public space. It was at a dive bar in Bushwick called *The Owls’ Nest*, where the bathroom had a picture of a bat taped to the ceiling that someone drew in Sharpie. I was 22, wearing a stolen blazer that smelled like cigarettes and regret, and I read a poem about my grandmother dying. Afterward, a man in the back who looked like a retired lumberjack—beard, flannel, the kind of hands that could palm bowling balls—clapped slowly and said, “Kid, that’s the first time I cried in a bar and didn’t feel like a faggot about it.” His name was Bob, and he became my regular after that. He brought me Jägermeister and told me stories about logging in the ‘80s. He died last year, and when I found out, I went to his favorite diner and ordered his usual: pancakes with bacon on the side, no syrup. The waitress recognized me and said, “You were his favorite.” I didn’t know I was anyone’s favorite until that moment.

That’s the power of being seen—not in a grand, earth-shattering way, but in the quiet, defiant way of someone recognizing you in the middle of a diner, ordering pancakes in memory of a man who taught you that grief doesn’t have to be pretty to be real.

I keep thinking about the phrase “quiet devastation.” It’s not the kind that makes headlines. It’s the kind that lives in the joints of your hands when you wake up at 4 AM unable to sleep. The kind that sits like a stone in your throat when you hear a song on the radio that your first love used to play on repeat. The kind that lives in the way you rearrange your apartment every six months, trying to outrun the ghosts, only to realize the ghosts have learned to fold themselves into the corners of the rooms.

I used to think dishwashers were gods. Then I lived with one that sounded like a dying vacuum cleaner and sprayed suds onto the ceiling during its spin cycle. Now I understand that even appliances have hidden depths of dysfunction.

Maybe that’s the whole point—nothing is ever just what it seems. A relationship isn’t just love; it’s love and resentment and unspoken needs and passive-aggressive text messages about who forgot to buy toilet paper. A city isn’t just buildings; it’s the cacophony of dialects bouncing off subway cars, the smell of pretzels mixed with urine, the way the dawn turns brick into something sacred for exactly six minutes before the trudge of daily life begins.

I’ve been in this apartment for six years. The walls are thin enough that I can hear my upstairs neighbor’s cat pacing at 2 AM, a tiny dictator policing the hours of darkness. I’ve named him Mr. Midnight. He hates me, I’m sure, but I leave a saucer of cream by the door every Thursday as a truce. Some days, I think my life is a series of small negotiations with the universe: feed the cat, don’t break the lease, write the words even when they’re ugly, take the subway to the doctor’s appointment even though the trains smell like a medieval plague pit.

Steve Martin has a bit where he says, “Some people have a way with words, and other people… oh… oh, uh, not have way.” I’m definitely in the latter category. But here’s the secret: not having a way with words doesn’t mean you don’t have something to say. It just means you say it clumsily, with your elbows out and your shoelaces untied.

And that’s okay.

Because life isn’t a well-organized essay. It’s more like a conversation over text at 2 AM: fragmented, with typos, half-finished sentences, sudden topics, and the occasional “LOL” when nothing is actually funny. The beauty is in the mess.

I’ve spent so much of my life trying to curate “the perfect” version of myself—the intellectual, the artist, the profound thinker—that I forgot that the real version is just… me. A person who loves Stanley the cat, who cries during sad movies but also during dog videos, who believes in ghosts but not in astrology (except when Mercury is in retrograde and chaos feels inevitable), who orders Thai food twice a week and has a habit of leaving socks on the bathroom floor like breadcrumbs for my future self to find.

I think if we were all truly honest about ourselves, the world wouldn’t need art at all. But since we’re not, art becomes the closest thing we have to a confession booth where the priest is kind of an asshole but sometimes changes his mind about forgiving you.

I don’t know what the point of all this is. Maybe there isn’t one. Maybe that’s the point.

But for now, I’ll keep writing badly. I’ll keep feeding Mr. Midnight. I’ll mail postcards to people who matter even if the postcards are blank. I’ll sit on the Hudson bench and watch the ferries make their orange trails on the water. I’ll apologize for the things I said in texts I sent at 3 AM. I’ll re-read these 2500 words tomorrow and cringe, but also feel something like recognition.

And in the end, that might be enough.
